description: We are forming a team in Ramallah to explore NASA’s open data and build a practical solution to a real-world problem. We welcome teammates interested in coding, data analysis, design, science, or storytelling. Our goal is to learn together, choose a focused challenge, and turn our idea into a working prototype. Beginners are welcome—curiosity, teamwork, and commitment matter!
summary: AstroCare is an offline health assistant for astronauts on exploration missions, where help from Earth may be delayed. It tracks daily readings, guides symptom assessment through an interactive body map and questions, flags reported warning signs, and saves a local health report. The prototype uses simulated data and is not a clinical diagnosis tool.
details: AstroCare is an offline health assistant for astronauts on exploration missions, where advice from Earth may be delayed or unavailable. A dashboard shows daily readings and measurement history in one view. For symptoms, the user selects a body region on an interactive body map and answers a series of questions. AstroCare then flags the warning signs they report, suggests possible causes using source-linked educational associations, and saves a local health report. The intended impact is to help a crew member record symptoms and recognize warning signs when immediate support is unavailable. It also lets them follow their own health data, and it is a foundation for preventive care. Core records and guidance work without internet, and optional voice features depend on browser support and an installed local language pack. The project is creative because it puts physical health and personal well-being in one offline app, with books, games and journaling for relaxation and reflection. We considered offline operation first. We also reviewed NASA information on spaceflight hazards and researched 20 health topics relevant to astronauts. We were careful about safety: the tool gives educational suggestions, not a diagnosis. All six daily readings are simulated, no hardware is connected, there is no clinical validation yet, and the demo records are not encrypted. We claim no NASA approval. Next, we plan to link games to astronauts’ daily tasks, expand reviewed clinical data and NASA evidence, evaluate machine learning, and validate the tool with space-medicine experts.
